claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Dou et al., 2003; Perez et al., 1991; Renkawek et al., 1994; Dabir et al., 2004; Sahara et al., 2007; Jinwal et al., 2013; Shimura et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Chaperones specifically recognize the six-residue aggregation-prone regions located at the start of the second and third repeats in the MTBR domain.
claims.source: The chaperones do so by specifically recognizing the six-residue aggregation-prone regions located at the start of the second and third repeats in the MTBR domain (Mok et al., 2018; Freilich et al., 2018; Baughman et al., 2018; Weickert et al., 2020; Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Mok et al., 2018; Freilich et al., 2018; Baughman et al., 2018; Weickert et al., 2020 and reference to Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The two motifs 275VQIINK280 (PHF6*) and 306VQIVYK311 (PHF6) are susceptible to the formation of β-sheet structures.
claims.source: These two motifs, 275VQIINK280 and 306VQIVYK311 (also called PHF6* and PHF6, respectively), are susceptible to the formation of β-sheet structures that have been found to be a prerequisite for tau aggregation (von Bergen et al., 2000; Mukrasch et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to von Bergen et al., 2000; Mukrasch et al., 2005.

claims.claim: β-sheet structures in PHF6* and PHF6 motifs are a prerequisite for tau aggregation.
claims.source: These two motifs, 275VQIINK280 and 306VQIVYK311 (also called PHF6* and PHF6, respectively), are susceptible to the formation of β-sheet structures that have been found to be a prerequisite for tau aggregation (von Bergen et al., 2000; Mukrasch et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to von Bergen et al., 2000; Mukrasch et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Hsp70 interaction with tau suppresses the formation of aggregation-prone tau nuclei.
claims.source: Hsp70 interaction with tau suppresses the formation of aggregation-prone tau nuclei and sequesters tau oligomers and fibrils (Baughman et al., 2018; Patterson et al., 2011), thereby neutralizing their ability to damage membranes and seed further tau aggregation (Kundel et al., 2018a).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Baughman et al., 2018; Patterson et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Hsp70 sequesters tau oligomers and fibrils.
claims.source: Hsp70 interaction with tau suppresses the formation of aggregation-prone tau nuclei and sequesters tau oligomers and fibrils (Baughman et al., 2018; Patterson et al., 2011), thereby neutralizing their ability to damage membranes and seed further tau aggregation (Kundel et al., 2018a).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Baughman et al., 2018; Patterson et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Hsp70 neutralizes the ability of tau oligomers and fibrils to damage membranes and seed further tau aggregation.
claims.source: Hsp70 interaction with tau suppresses the formation of aggregation-prone tau nuclei and sequesters tau oligomers and fibrils (Baughman et al., 2018; Patterson et al., 2011), thereby neutralizing their ability to damage membranes and seed further tau aggregation (Kundel et al., 2018a).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kundel et al., 2018a.

claims.claim: HSPB1 delays tau fiber formation by weakly interacting with early species in the aggregation reaction.
claims.source: In contrast, HSPB1 was shown to delay tau fiber formation by weakly interacting with early species in the aggregation reaction (Baughman et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Baughman et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Members of the Hsp40 family have been reported to affect tau aggregation in the cell.
claims.source: Excitingly, though, HSPB1 is not the only ATP-independent chaperone reported to interfere with the tau aggregation pathway – members of the Hsp40 family (also known as J-domain proteins [JDPs]) have also recently been reported to affect tau aggregation in the cell (Mok et al., 2018; Brehme et al., 2014; Fontaine et al., 2015; Hou et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Mok et al., 2018; Brehme et al., 2014; Fontaine et al., 2015; Hou et al., 2020.

claims.claim: JDPs function as co-chaperones of the Hsp70 machinery.
claims.source: JDPs are a diverse group of proteins that function as co-chaperones of the Hsp70 machinery, and are responsible both for selecting and delivering clients to the chaperones, and stimulating Hsp70 ATPase activity, thereby activating the chaperone cycle.
claims.evidence: Stated as established knowledge about JDP function.

claims.claim: JDPs are responsible for selecting and delivering clients to Hsp70 chaperones.
claims.source: JDPs are a diverse group of proteins that function as co-chaperones of the Hsp70 machinery, and are responsible both for selecting and delivering clients to the chaperones, and stimulating Hsp70 ATPase activity, thereby activating the chaperone cycle.
claims.evidence: Stated as established knowledge about JDP function.

claims.claim: JDPs stimulate Hsp70 ATPase activity.
claims.source: JDPs are a diverse group of proteins that function as co-chaperones of the Hsp70 machinery, and are responsible both for selecting and delivering clients to the chaperones, and stimulating Hsp70 ATPase activity, thereby activating the chaperone cycle.
claims.evidence: Stated as established knowledge about JDP function.

claims.claim: All JDPs are structurally characterized by the conserved signature J-domain.
claims.source: These multidomain proteins are all structurally characterized by the conserved signature J-domain, essential for stimulation of Hsp70 ATPase activity (Kityk et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kityk et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The J-domain is essential for stimulation of Hsp70 ATPase activity.
claims.source: These multidomain proteins are all structurally characterized by the conserved signature J-domain, essential for stimulation of Hsp70 ATPase activity (Kityk et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kityk et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Canonical class A and B JDPs comprise a regulatory glycine‐rich (GF) region adjacent to the N-terminal J-domain.
claims.source: In addition, canonical class A and B JDPs also comprise a regulatory glycine‐rich (GF) region adjacent to the N-terminal J-domain (Faust et al., 2020; Karamanos et al., 2019), two structurally similar C-terminal β‐barrel domains (CTDI and CTDII) containing the substrate binding region, and a dimerization domain (Kampinga and Craig, 2010; Rosenzweig et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Faust et al., 2020; Karamanos et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Canonical class A and B JDPs comprise two structurally similar C-terminal β‐barrel domains (CTDI and CTDII) containing the substrate binding region.
claims.source: In addition, canonical class A and B JDPs also comprise a regulatory glycine‐rich (GF) region adjacent to the N-terminal J-domain (Faust et al., 2020; Karamanos et al., 2019), two structurally similar C-terminal β‐barrel domains (CTDI and CTDII) containing the substrate binding region, and a dimerization domain (Kampinga and Craig, 2010; Rosenzweig et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Kampinga and Craig, 2010; Rosenzweig et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Canonical class A and B JDPs comprise a dimerization domain.
claims.source: In addition, canonical class A and B JDPs also comprise a regulatory glycine‐rich (GF) region adjacent to the N-terminal J-domain (Faust et al., 2020; Karamanos et al., 2019), two structurally similar C-terminal β‐barrel domains (CTDI and CTDII) containing the substrate binding region, and a dimerization domain (Kampinga and Craig, 2010; Rosenzweig et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Kampinga and Craig, 2010; Rosenzweig et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Class A JDPs contain a zinc-finger-like region (ZFLR) protruding from CTDI.
claims.source: Class A JDPs further contain a zinc-finger-like region (ZFLR) protruding from CTDI.
claims.evidence: Stated as established knowledge about class A JDP structure.

claims.claim: JDPs can function as bona fide chaperones, utilizing holdase activity to prevent the aggregation of their client proteins.
claims.source: Recently, several studies have indicated that JDPs can also function as bona fide chaperones, utilizing holdase activity to prevent the aggregation of their client proteins (Ayala Mariscal and Kirstein, 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Ayala Mariscal and Kirstein, 2021.

claims.claim: DNAJA2 was identified as a potent suppressor of tau aggregation.
claims.source: DNAJA2, a member of this JDP family, was recently identified as a potent suppressor of tau aggregation, capable of effectively preventing the seeding of tau and formation of amyloids in cells (Mok et al., 2018; Abisambra et al., 2012), with DNAJA2 levels being selectively increased in AD patient neuronal cells (Mok et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Mok et al., 2018; Abisambra et al., 2012.

claims.claim: DNAJA2 is capable of effectively preventing the seeding of tau and formation of amyloids in cells.
claims.source: DNAJA2, a member of this JDP family, was recently identified as a potent suppressor of tau aggregation, capable of effectively preventing the seeding of tau and formation of amyloids in cells (Mok et al., 2018; Abisambra et al., 2012), with DNAJA2 levels being selectively increased in AD patient neuronal cells (Mok et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Mok et al., 2018; Abisambra et al., 2012.

claims.claim: DNAJA2 levels are selectively increased in AD patient neuronal cells.
claims.source: DNAJA2, a member of this JDP family, was recently identified as a potent suppressor of tau aggregation, capable of effectively preventing the seeding of tau and formation of amyloids in cells (Mok et al., 2018; Abisambra et al., 2012), with DNAJA2 levels being selectively increased in AD patient neuronal cells (Mok et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Mok et al., 2018.

claims.claim: DNAJB1, along with the Hsp70 system, can break apart tau amyloid fibers extracted from AD brain tissues.
claims.source: Additionally, it was recently shown that, along with the Hsp70 system, DNAJB1, a class B JDP, can break apart tau amyloid fibers extracted from AD brain tissues (Nachman et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Nachman et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Addition of HSPB1 significantly inhibited tau fiber formation.
claims.source: As expected, the addition of HSPB1 significantly inhibited tau fiber formation, in agreement with previous reports (Mok et al., 2018; Freilich et al., 2018; Baughman et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Mok et al., 2018; Freilich et al., 2018; Baughman et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Addition of DNAJA2 and DNAJB1 chaperones completely inhibited the formation of tau fibrils for over 16 hr.
claims.source: Interestingly, addition of DNAJA2 and DNAJB1 chaperones also completely inhibited the formation of tau fibrils for over 16 hr (Figure 1B), with no observable ThT signal being detected over this length of time.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Tau4R aggregates faster than full-length tau (t½ ≈ 110 min vs. t½ ≈ 340 min).
claims.source: Despite the faster aggregation kinetics of tau4R relative to the full-length tau (t½ ≈ 110 min vs. t½ ≈ 340 min), the presence of even a sub-stoichiometric concentration of either of the three molecular chaperones (DNAJB1, HSPB1, or DNAJA2) fully suppressed aggregation for the duration of the experiment (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Sub-stoichiometric concentrations of DNAJB1, HSPB1, or DNAJA2 fully suppressed tau4R aggregation.
claims.source: Despite the faster aggregation kinetics of tau4R relative to the full-length tau (t½ ≈ 110 min vs. t½ ≈ 340 min), the presence of even a sub-stoichiometric concentration of either of the three molecular chaperones (DNAJB1, HSPB1, or DNAJA2) fully suppressed aggregation for the duration of the experiment (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: HSPB1 binds to tau residues 275–280 and 306–311, which correspond to the PHF6* and PHF6 motifs.
claims.source: Upon addition of HSPB1, we observed significant peak broadening of tau residues 275–280 and 306–311, which correspond to the PHF6* and PHF6 motifs (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), in agreement with previous reports (Mok et al., 2018; Freilich et al., 2018; Baughman et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and citations to Mok et al., 2018; Freilich et al., 2018; Baughman et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The PHF6 motifs are the most hydrophobic regions within tau.
claims.source: Notably, the PHF6 motifs, which are the most hydrophobic regions within tau, are also the preferential binding sites for the major ATP-dependent chaperone families, such as Hsp70 and Hsp90 (Mok et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Mok et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The PHF6 motifs are the preferential binding sites for Hsp70 and Hsp90 chaperones.
claims.source: Notably, the PHF6 motifs, which are the most hydrophobic regions within tau, are also the preferential binding sites for the major ATP-dependent chaperone families, such as Hsp70 and Hsp90 (Mok et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Mok et al., 2018.

claims.claim: DNAJA2 binds to tau residues 275–284 and 306–320, showing a preference for the PHF6 and PHF6* motifs.
claims.source: A similar preference for the PHF6 and PHF6* motifs was also found for DNAJA2, with residues 275–284 and 306–320 showing significant peak broadening (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: DNAJB1 showed no significant binding to tau monomers.
claims.source: Surprisingly, however, DNAJB1 showed no significant binding to tau, despite efficiently suppressing amyloid formation (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A large portion of DNAJB1 co-precipitated with tau4R fibrils in co-sedimentation experiments.
claims.source: Indeed, a large portion of DNAJB1 was detected in the insoluble fraction together with tau4R (Figure 2A), indicating a strong interaction between tau fibrils and the chaperone.
claims.evidence: Supported by co-sedimentation data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: DNAJA2 co-precipitated with tau fibers in co-sedimentation experiments.
claims.source: Co-sedimentation experiments with DNAJA2 and HSPB1 showed that also DNAJA2 co-precipitated with tau fibers, whereas HSPB1 was mainly found in the soluble fraction and only marginally interacted with tau amyloids (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by co-sedimentation data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: HSPB1 was mainly found in the soluble fraction and only marginally interacted with tau amyloids.
claims.source: Co-sedimentation experiments with DNAJA2 and HSPB1 showed that also DNAJA2 co-precipitated with tau fibers, whereas HSPB1 was mainly found in the soluble fraction and only marginally interacted with tau amyloids (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by co-sedimentation data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The dissociation constant (KD) for DNAJB1 binding to tau4R fibrils is 1.7 ± 0.2 µM.
claims.source: Similar results were also obtained with fluorescence anisotropy, resulting in an affinity (dissociation constant) for tau4R fibrils of 1.7 ± 0.2 µM (mean ± s.e.m.) for DNAJB1 and of 7.6 ± 0.6 µM for DNAJA2 (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The dissociation constant (KD) for DNAJA2 binding to tau4R fibrils is 7.6 ± 0.6 µM.
claims.source: Similar results were also obtained with fluorescence anisotropy, resulting in an affinity (dissociation constant) for tau4R fibrils of 1.7 ± 0.2 µM (mean ± s.e.m.) for DNAJB1 and of 7.6 ± 0.6 µM for DNAJA2 (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The affinity of HSPB1 for tau fibers was outside the experimental concentration range.
claims.source: In contrast, the affinity of HSPB1 for tau fibers was outside our experimental concentration range.
claims.evidence: Stated based on experimental observations.

claims.claim: Tau alone forms characteristic long twisted filaments with a periodicity of 50–100 nm.
claims.source: Here, tau alone formed characteristic long twisted filaments with a periodicity of 50–100 nm (Figure 2D), consistent with previous observations (Fitzpatrick et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by EM data shown in Figure 2D and citation to Fitzpatrick et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Addition of HSPB1 to tau fibers caused no changes to fiber length or morphology.
claims.source: Upon addition of HSPB1 chaperone to the fibers, no changes to fiber length or morphology were detected, in agreement with our co-sedimentation assays that showed no binding of HSPB1 chaperone to the preformed fibers.
claims.evidence: Supported by EM observations and co-sedimentation data.

claims.claim: HSPB1 generates large protein assemblies.
claims.source: HSPB1 itself, however, generated large protein assemblies that can be seen next to the fibers in the EM images (marked by *).
claims.evidence: Supported by EM data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Addition of DNAJB1 or DNAJA2 caused visible change in the appearance of tau fibers, generating straighter, less twisted filaments decorated by periodically bound chaperones.
claims.source: Addition of DNAJB1 or DNAJA2, on the other hand, caused visible change in the appearance of the fibers, generating straighter, less twisted filaments decorated by periodically bound chaperones (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: Supported by EM data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: DNAJB1 and DNAJA2 do not enhance fiber breakage or fragmentation upon binding.
claims.source: The overall length of the fibers, however, did not change substantially, and also smaller tau fragments were not observed in our EM images, indicating that DNAJB1 and DNAJA2 do not enhance fiber breakage or fragmentation upon binding.
claims.evidence: Inferred from EM observations showing no change in fiber length or presence of smaller fragments.

claims.claim: HSPB1 only binds tau4R monomers.
claims.source: In summary, HSPB1 only binds tau4R monomers, DNAJB1 interacts with tau4R fibrils, whereas DNAJA2 binds both monomers and fibers (Figure 2B, C).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 2B, C.

claims.claim: DNAJB1 interacts with tau4R fibrils.
claims.source: In summary, HSPB1 only binds tau4R monomers, DNAJB1 interacts with tau4R fibrils, whereas DNAJA2 binds both monomers and fibers (Figure 2B, C).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 2B, C.

claims.claim: DNAJA2 binds both tau4R monomers and fibers.
claims.source: In summary, HSPB1 only binds tau4R monomers, DNAJB1 interacts with tau4R fibrils, whereas DNAJA2 binds both monomers and fibers (Figure 2B, C).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 2B, C.

claims.claim: The aggregation of tau4R occurs through primary nucleation, fibril growth through saturating elongation, and fiber fragmentation.
claims.source: In the absence of chaperones, the aggregation of tau4R has previously been reported to occur through the following microscopic steps: primary nucleation, fibril growth through the addition and rearrangement of monomers (saturating elongation), and fiber fragmentation (Kundel et al., 2018b; Yao et al., 2020; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Kundel et al., 2018b; Yao et al., 2020 and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The scaling exponent for tau4R aggregation was −0.34 ± 0.04, consistent with a dominant primary nucleation pathway and a contribution from fibril fragmentation.
claims.source: This was found to be −0.34 ± 0.04, which was consistent with a dominant primary nucleation pathway and a contribution stemming from the presence of fibril fragmentation (Kundel et al., 2018b; Yao et al., 2020; Shammas et al., 2015; see Materials and methods for more detail).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Kundel et al., 2018b; Yao et al., 2020; Shammas et al., 2015.

claims.claim: All chaperones caused a concentration-dependent retardation of tau aggregation at sub-stoichiometric concentrations.
claims.source: All chaperones caused a concentration-dependent retardation of tau aggregation at sub-stoichiometric concentrations (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: HSPB1 primarily affects the elongation rate in tau aggregation kinetics.
claims.source: Upon fitting HSPB1 aggregation-prevention data, only a poor agreement was achieved when allowing the perturbation of primary nucleation rates (kn) (Figure 3A). Given the fact that HSPB1 binds tau monomers, the relatively moderate effect on tau primary nucleation was somewhat surprising as monomer binding should inhibit both nucleation and elongation. In contrast, fitting the fiber elongation rate (kp) provided a significantly better description of the kinetic data (Figure 3A), indicating an order of magnitude reduction of this rate (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: Supported by kinetic fitting data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3D.

claims.claim: DNAJA2 affects both tau nucleation and elongation rates.
claims.source: The effect of DNAJA2 on tau aggregation could neither be described by the reduction of nucleation rates nor elongation rates alone (Figure 3B), which is not entirely surprising, given that the chaperone can bind to both monomeric tau and fibrils (Figure 1D, Figure 2B, C).
claims.evidence: Supported by kinetic fitting data shown in Figure 3B and binding data in Figure 1D, Figure 2B, C.

claims.claim: DNAJB1 primarily affects the rate of tau primary nucleation.
claims.source: Surprisingly, the effect of DNAJB1 on tau aggregation was best described by its ability to reduce the rates of primary nucleation (Figure 3C, left) and, only to a lesser extent, fiber elongation (Figure 3C, right).
claims.evidence: Supported by kinetic fitting data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Soluble monomeric tau4R exists in two conformational ensembles – an 'inert' tau monomer and a seed-competent monomer.
claims.source: The effect of DNAJB1 on tau4R nucleation, despite its inability to interact with monomeric tau4R, can, however, be reconciled by the recent finding that soluble monomeric tau4R exists in two conformational ensembles – an ensemble that does not spontaneously aggregate ('inert' tau monomer) and a seed-competent monomer that triggers the spontaneous aggregation of tau (Mirbaha et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Mirbaha et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Seed-competent tau species are readily populated in tauopathy-associated tau mutants.
claims.source: Such seed-competent species have been proposed to be readily populated in tauopathy-associated tau mutants (Chen et al., 2019), and can be generated in vitro by addition of polyanions such as heparin (Eschmann et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2019 and Eschmann et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Seed-competent tau species can be generated in vitro by addition of polyanions such as heparin.
claims.source: Such seed-competent species have been proposed to be readily populated in tauopathy-associated tau mutants (Chen et al., 2019), and can be generated in vitro by addition of polyanions such as heparin (Eschmann et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Eschmann et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Low concentrations of heparin enhance the rate of tau fiber formation.
claims.source: Low concentrations of heparin enhance the rate of fiber formation, whereas higher heparin concentrations potentially inhibit it (Ramachandran and Udgaonkar, 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Ramachandran and Udgaonkar, 2011.

claims.claim: Higher heparin concentrations inhibit tau fiber formation.
claims.source: Low concentrations of heparin enhance the rate of fiber formation, whereas higher heparin concentrations potentially inhibit it (Ramachandran and Udgaonkar, 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Ramachandran and Udgaonkar, 2011.

claims.claim: Heparin increased the rate of tau fiber formation up to a sub-stoichiometric concentration of 1 µM.
claims.source: We found that heparin increased the rate of fiber formation up to a sub-stoichiometric concentration of 1 µM (1:0.1 tau:heparin) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: At one- to fourfold excess of heparin (10–40 µM), tau amyloid formation was arrested for over 2 hr.
claims.source: At a one- to fourfold excess of heparin (10–40 µM), we found that tau amyloid formation was arrested for over 2 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Heparin binding to tau results in chemical shift perturbations mainly in the R1, R2, and PHF6* regions.
claims.source: Heparin binding resulted in chemical shift perturbations (CSPs) to the NMR spectrum of tau4R, mainly in the R1, R2, and PHF6* regions (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Heparin binding does not induce global folding of tau.
claims.source: No changes were observed to the overall dispersion of the spectrum, indicating that heparin binding does not induce global folding of tau, in agreement with previous findings (Mukrasch et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR observations and citation to Mukrasch et al., 2005.

claims.claim: DNAJB1 interacts strongly with the aggregation-prone tau-heparin species.
claims.source: With these assignments in hand, we were able to identify that, despite having negligible affinity toward the tau monomer, the DNAJB1 chaperone indeed interacts strongly with the aggregation-prone tau-heparin mixture (Figure 4B), as we previously predicted.
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: DNAJB1 binds to tau residues 275–280 and 305–314 of the PHF6 and PHF6* repeats in the aggregation-prone tau-heparin species.
claims.source: We further mapped this binding to tau residues 275–280 and 305–314 of the PHF6 and PHF6* repeats – the same regions to which both DNAJA2 and HSPB1 bind in the inert, monomeric tau.
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR mapping data.

claims.claim: DNAJA2 shows strong binding to the R2 and R3 PHF6* repeats of aggregation-prone tau4R.
claims.source: DNAJA2 showed strong binding to the R2 and R3 PHF6* repeats of this aggregation-prone form of tau4R, similarly to its interaction with the free monomer (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: HSPB1 only binds weakly to the aggregation-prone tau-heparin species.
claims.source: In contrast, HSPB1 only bound this species weakly, despite previously displaying a strong interaction with free tau4R.
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR observations.

claims.claim: The lack of interaction between HSPB1 and aggregation-prone tau species explains why HSPB1 does not affect the rate of fiber nucleation.
claims.source: The lack of interaction between HSPB1 and aggregation-prone tau species explains our previous observation that HSPB1 does not affect the rate of fiber nucleation (Figure 3A), as such an inhibition would require a direct interaction with the aggregate nucleus or aggregation-prone tau.
claims.evidence: Inferred from binding data and kinetic data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: HSPB1 interacts solely with tau monomers.
claims.source: Thus, while interacting with the same regions of tau, the three chaperones each display specific preferences for the different tau monomer conformers: HSPB1 interacts solely with tau monomers; DNAJB1 exclusively with the aggregation-prone species; and DNAJA2 with both.
claims.evidence: Summarized from binding experiments.

claims.claim: DNAJB1 interacts exclusively with the aggregation-prone tau species.
claims.source: Thus, while interacting with the same regions of tau, the three chaperones each display specific preferences for the different tau monomer conformers: HSPB1 interacts solely with tau monomers; DNAJB1 exclusively with the aggregation-prone species; and DNAJA2 with both.
claims.evidence: Summarized from binding experiments.

claims.claim: DNAJA2 interacts with both inert tau monomers and aggregation-prone tau species.
claims.source: Thus, while interacting with the same regions of tau, the three chaperones each display specific preferences for the different tau monomer conformers: HSPB1 interacts solely with tau monomers; DNAJB1 exclusively with the aggregation-prone species; and DNAJA2 with both.
claims.evidence: Summarized from binding experiments.

claims.claim: The PHF6 repeats in tau display no increase in secondary-structure propensity upon addition of heparin.
claims.source: Secondary-structure propensity analysis (Marsh et al., 2006) of free and heparin-bound tau demonstrated that the different chaperone binding profiles cannot be explained by heparin-induced formation of extended β-strand structures in the PHF6 repeats (Eschmann et al., 2017) as these regions displayed no increase in secondary-structure propensity upon addition of heparin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by secondary structure propensity analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Electrostatic interactions cannot explain the different binding profiles of the chaperones to the two tau species.
claims.source: Screening any such electrostatic interactions with higher ionic strengths (0.3 M), however, neither facilitated binding between DNAJB1 and tau4R (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) nor altered tau4R interaction with HSPB1 or DNAJA2 chaperones (compare Figure 1D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2). Similarly, the interaction cannot be explained by attractive electrostatic interactions caused by the negative net-charge of the complex as we did not detect specific binding between heparin and any of the chaperones. Hence, electrostatic interactions cannot explain the different binding profiles of the chaperones to the two tau species.
claims.evidence: Supported by high salt NMR experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Patient-derived, seeding-competent tau monomer has an expanded ensemble with a more exposed PHF6 motif compared to the inert monomeric protein.
claims.source: A clue to how heparin alters the conformational ensemble of tau4R came from a recent structural characterization of patient-derived, seeding-competent tau monomer. This species of tau was reported to have an expanded ensemble with a more exposed PHF6 motif compared to the inert monomeric protein (Mirbaha et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Mirbaha et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Increased expansion of the PHF6 aggregation motifs drives the self-assembly and subsequent aggregation of tau.
claims.source: This increased expansion of the PHF6 aggregation motifs was, in turn, suggested to drive the self-assembly and subsequent aggregation of tau (Kaufman et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kaufman et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Binding of heparin to tau expands the local conformation of the repeat regions (R2 and R3), making the amyloidogenic PHF6 sequences more accessible.
claims.source: Interestingly, binding of heparin to tau was also shown to expand the local conformation of the repeat regions (R2 and R3), thereby making the amyloidogenic PHF6 sequences more accessible (Eschmann et al., 2017).

results.result: HSPB1, DNAJA2, and DNAJB1 chaperones all suppress tau aggregation in vitro. All three chaperones completely inhibited tau fibril formation at sub-stoichiometric concentrations for over 16 hours, with tau4R aggregating faster than full-length tau.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C45 are supported by ThT fluorescence aggregation assays (Figure 1B, C) showing complete suppression of tau aggregation by all three chaperones. The data are consistent with prior literature and demonstrate reproducible inhibition across multiple tau constructs.

results.result: The three chaperones display distinct binding preferences for tau species: HSPB1 binds only monomeric tau at PHF6/PHF6* motifs, DNAJB1 shows no binding to monomers, and DNAJA2 binds both monomers and fibrils at the same motifs.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C64 are supported by NMR spectroscopy (Figure 1D, Figure 2B-C) and fluorescence anisotropy measurements showing differential binding patterns. The NMR peak broadening data clearly demonstrate HSPB1 and DNAJA2 binding to monomers while DNAJB1 does not, consistent with subsequent functional data.

results.result: DNAJB1 and DNAJA2 bind preformed tau fibrils with micromolar affinity (KD = 1.7 ± 0.2 µM and 7.6 ± 0.6 µM, respectively), while HSPB1 shows minimal fibril binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C56 are supported by co-sedimentation assays (Figure 2A) and fluorescence anisotropy measurements (Figure 2B) providing quantitative binding affinities. The data are internally consistent and demonstrate clear differences in fibril-binding capacity among the three chaperones.

results.result: Electron microscopy reveals that DNAJB1 and DNAJA2 binding alters tau fiber morphology, producing straighter filaments decorated with chaperones, while HSPB1 does not change fiber morphology but forms separate protein assemblies.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C61 are supported by negative stain EM images (Figure 2D) showing distinct morphological changes. The observations are consistent with the binding data and provide visual confirmation of chaperone-fibril interactions. However, the claim that chaperones do not enhance fragmentation (C61) is based on absence of evidence rather than direct measurement.

results.result: Tau4R aggregation proceeds through primary nucleation, saturating elongation, and fragmentation, with a scaling exponent of −0.34 ± 0.04. All three chaperones cause concentration-dependent retardation of aggregation at sub-stoichiometric concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 are supported by concentration-dependent aggregation kinetics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and kinetic modeling consistent with prior literature. The scaling exponent analysis follows established methodology and the data quality appears sufficient for the conclusions drawn.

results.result: The three chaperones affect different microscopic steps in tau aggregation: HSPB1 primarily reduces elongation rates, DNAJB1 primarily reduces nucleation rates, and DNAJA2 affects both nucleation and elongation.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 are supported by global fitting of kinetic data to mechanistic models (Figure 3A-D). The fits show good agreement with experimental data and residuals are reasonable. The use of seeded and unseeded experiments for DNAJA2 strengthens the analysis, though the model assumes chaperones don't affect ThT accessibility.

results.result: Tau exists in two conformational states: an inert monomer and an aggregation-prone species. DNAJB1 selectively binds the aggregation-prone tau-heparin complex at PHF6/PHF6* motifs, while HSPB1 binds weakly to this species, explaining their differential effects on nucleation.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C87 are supported by NMR experiments with heparin-bound tau (Figure 4A-B) showing DNAJB1 binding to the aggregation-prone species. The use of heparin to generate a stable aggregation-prone species is well-justified, and the NMR assignments (88% complete) provide confidence in the binding site mapping. The interpretation reconciles the paradox of DNAJB1 affecting nucleation without binding monomers.

results.result: Heparin exhibits biphasic effects on tau aggregation: low concentrations (≤1 µM) accelerate aggregation while higher concentrations (10-40 µM) arrest it for over 2 hours. Heparin binding causes chemical shift perturbations in R1, R2, and PHF6* regions without inducing global folding.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 are supported by concentration-dependent aggregation assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and NMR chemical shift perturbation analysis (Figure 4A). The biphasic effect is clearly demonstrated and the NMR data confirm localized binding without global structural changes, consistent with prior literature.

results.result: The differential chaperone binding to inert versus aggregation-prone tau cannot be explained by secondary structure changes or electrostatic interactions, as demonstrated by secondary structure propensity analysis and high-salt NMR experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 are supported by secondary structure propensity calculations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and high-salt binding experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). These control experiments effectively rule out two plausible alternative explanations for the differential binding, strengthening the conformational expansion hypothesis.

results.result: The PHF6 regions in aggregation-prone tau adopt an expanded conformation compared to inert monomers, as evidenced by reduced RDC values in heparin-bound tau. This expansion enables DNAJB1 binding by increasing PHF6 accessibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C95 are supported by RDC measurements in multiple alignment media (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-C) showing large RDCs (10-20 Hz) in free tau PHF6 regions but small RDCs in tau-heparin complex despite higher alignment. The interpretation is consistent with prior structural studies and provides a mechanistic explanation for DNAJB1 selectivity.

results.result: P301L/S tauopathy mutants contain a higher population of expanded PHF6 conformation, enabling DNAJB1 binding to monomers. All three chaperones suppress P301L/S aggregation, but HSPB1 shows reduced efficacy while DNAJB1 shows enhanced activity compared to wild-type tau.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C103 are supported by RDC measurements (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D-E), NMR binding studies (Figure 4C), and aggregation assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B-C) with P301L/S mutants. The degree of NMR intensity reduction (26-31%) is consistent with the reported low population of expanded conformers, providing quantitative support for the conformational selection model.

results.result: DNAJA2 and DNAJB1 produce dose-dependent reductions in tau fibril length and mass, with DNAJA2 being more effective (88% reduction at 0.5:1 ratio) than DNAJB1 (67% reduction). HSPB1 is less effective, showing only 45% mass reduction at 1:1 ratio and unable to completely suppress fiber formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C113 are supported by EM imaging (Figure 5A-C) and kinetic measurements (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The quantitative mass reduction data are consistent with the EM observations of shorter fibrils. The comparison across chaperones is internally consistent with their differential binding properties and effects on microscopic rates.

results.result: DNAJA2 uses two distinct binding sites: CTDI binds inert tau monomers (KD = 43 µM) in fast exchange, while CTDII preferentially binds aggregation-prone tau species. DNAJB1 shows no CTDI binding to monomers despite 56% sequence identity with DNAJA2 CTDI.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C119 are supported by NMR chemical shift perturbation and intensity measurements on labeled chaperone constructs (Figure 6A-D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The use of monomeric Ydj1 constructs is well-justified for NMR, and the differential binding to CTDI vs CTDII is clearly demonstrated. The lack of DNAJB1-monomer binding despite high CTDI homology is a key mechanistic insight.

results.result: Both DNAJB1 and DNAJA2 recognize aggregation-prone tau predominantly via CTDII, with structural differences in CTDI likely explaining their divergent specificities for different tau species.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C123 are supported by NMR data showing CTDII binding for both chaperones (Figure 6F-G). The inference about CTDI structural differences (C123) is reasonable given the binding data but is not directly demonstrated structurally. The parallel with α-synuclein binding (C121) suggests CTDII may be a general amyloid-binding site.

results.result: DNAJA2's ability to simultaneously interact with multiple tau species (monomers via CTDI, aggregation-prone species and fibers via CTDII) explains its high effectiveness in aggregation prevention and potential role as an early protective factor.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C128 integrate binding data, kinetic analysis, and EM observations to explain DNAJA2's superior aggregation prevention. The mechanistic model is well-supported by the data, though the inference about cellular protective function (C128) extends beyond the in vitro data. The correlation with AD pathology is cited but not directly tested.

results.result: DNAJB1 functions as a bona fide chaperone by preventing seeding nuclei formation and binding mature fibers to slow growth. Its CTDII-mediated interactions leave CTDI free to potentially recruit Hsp70 for disaggregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C131 are supported by the kinetic analysis showing nucleation inhibition and the binding data showing fibril association. The inference about CTDI availability for Hsp70 recruitment (C131) is logical given the CTDII binding but is speculative and not directly tested. The model is consistent with prior work on DNAJB1-mediated disaggregation.

results.result: HSPB1's limitation to monomer binding restricts it to inhibiting elongation, resulting in limited prevention of tau amyloid formation. In contrast, Hsp40 chaperones' ability to bind forming fibers and aggregation-prone species enables more effective aggregation prevention.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C135 synthesize the mechanistic findings to explain differential chaperone efficacy. The conclusions are well-supported by the integrated binding, kinetic, and EM data. The comparison highlights how binding specificity determines functional outcome in aggregation prevention.

results.result: HSPB1 shows reduced activity against P301L tau mutant, while DNAJA2 and DNAJB1 remain effective, with DNAJB1 showing even higher activity against this tauopathy mutant.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C137 are supported by aggregation assays comparing wild-type and P301L tau (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B-C). The differential effects are consistent with the conformational selection model, where the expanded conformation in P301L reduces HSPB1 affinity but enhances DNAJB1 binding. This has important implications for therapeutic targeting of tauopathies.

results.result: Chaperone-mediated disaggregation may generate seeding-competent low-molecular-weight tau species, potentially contributing to prion-like propagation of tau pathology rather than being purely beneficial.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C140 are largely speculative. C138 is supported by citation to prior work, but C139-C140 are hypotheses about potential negative consequences of chaperone activity that are not tested in this study. The authors appropriately present these as possibilities requiring further investigation, but no direct evidence for prion-like propagation is provided.

results.result: HSPB1 may be more beneficial than Hsp40s for slowing disease progression because it doesn't generate smaller tau species. However, coupling to degradation pathways could render Hsp40 activity beneficial by enabling clearance of smaller fibrils and aggregation-prone monomers.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C143 are speculative discussions of potential cellular outcomes. C141 is inferred from EM data showing no smaller species with HSPB1, but the therapeutic implications are not tested. C142-C143 discuss degradation pathways that were not examined in this study. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future work but lack direct experimental support.
